case_info.scenario: A 52-year-old presented to the rheumatology clinic with 3 weeks of pain and duskiness of the fingertips bilaterally. The patient reported no dyspnea, cough, nasal discharge, diarrhea weight loss, or fevers. She had no history of rheumatologic disease or Raynaud disease, did not smoke cigarettes, take daily medications, ingest raw meat, or report recent travel. On presentation, her temperature was 98.2 °F (36.8 °C); blood pressure, 132/70 mm Hg; heart rate, 86/min; and oxygen saturation, 99% on room air. Findings on the physical examination were normal, other than her fingertips, which were cold and cyanotic with small ulcerations on the second and third fingertips (Figure). White blood cell count was 25.1 × 109/L (reference range, 3.8-9.8 × 109/L) and manual differential revealed 74.5% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count, 18.7 × 109/L) and no blasts. Hemoglobin level and platelet count were normal. D-dimer level was 1.5 μg/mL (8.21 nmol/L) (reference range, 0.0-0.99 μg/mL [0.0-5.42 nmol/L]). Test results were negative for antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase, and HIV. Results of computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and of flexible nasopharyngoscopy, were normal.

case_info.caption: The patient’s cyanotic and ulcerated fingertips at presentation.
case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree that arterial Doppler is the most appropriate next step. With an absolute eosinophil count this high (>1.5 x 10^9/L) and digital necrosis, the priority is to rule out hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) and its associated cardiac or thromboembolic complications. The next critical step is to obtain an echocardiogram to evaluate for endomyocardial involvement and cardiac thrombus, which is a key cause of morbidity in HES.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

case_info.scenario: A 52-year-old presented to the rheumatology clinic with 3 weeks of pain and duskiness of the fingertips bilaterally. The patient reported no dyspnea, cough, nasal discharge, diarrhea weight loss, or fevers. She had no history of rheumatologic disease or Raynaud disease, did not smoke cigarettes, take daily medications, ingest raw meat, or report recent travel. On presentation, her temperature was 98.2 °F (36.8 °C); blood pressure, 132/70 mm Hg; heart rate, 86/min; and oxygen saturation, 99% on room air. Findings on the physical examination were normal, other than her fingertips, which were cold and cyanotic with small ulcerations on the second and third fingertips (Figure). White blood cell count was 25.1 × 109/L (reference range, 3.8-9.8 × 109/L) and manual differential revealed 74.5% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count, 18.7 × 109/L) and no blasts. Hemoglobin level and platelet count were normal. D-dimer level was 1.5 μg/mL (8.21 nmol/L) (reference range, 0.0-0.99 μg/mL [0.0-5.42 nmol/L]). Test results were negative for antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase, and HIV. Results of computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and of flexible nasopharyngoscopy, were normal.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

The patient reported no dyspnea, cough, nasal discharge, diarrhea weight loss, or fevers. Hemoglobin level and platelet count were normal. D-dimer level was 1.5 μg/mL (8.21 nmol/L) (reference range, 0.0-0.99 μg/mL [0.0-5.42 nmol/L]). Test results were negative for antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase, and HIV. Results of computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and of flexible nasopharyngoscopy, were normal.
